processing: As with other sheng pu-erh, large-leaf leaf is wok-fixed, rolled and sun-dried, then sold loose or pressed. Nothing documented sets a separate local method.
harvest_season: Spring is usually the prized picking, as is typical in Yunnan.
appearance_dry: Typical of Yunnan sheng: long dark green leaf with some pale buds.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow when young, as is typical of sheng.
appearance_wet: As with other large-leaf sheng, thick olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: Little is documented about a regional taste. Expect what is typical of young large-leaf sheng: fresh and woody with some bitterness that gives way to sweetness.

brewing.notes: Usual young sheng approach: quick rinse, short early steeps.

vintage_note: Sold as is usual for regional sheng: by harvest year, mostly young, loose or pressed. Aged Dehong is rarely seen. A named county or village is worth more than the region's name.
description:
Dehong is a prefecture on Yunnan's western border with Myanmar, and its pu-erh is a minor name on the map. Production is sparser here than in Lincang or Xishuangbanna, so most drinkers will not meet it by chance.

The tea grows mainly in Mangshi, Ruili, Lianghe, Yingjiang and Longchuan. Method is the usual one for sheng, and nothing documented sets a separate local style.

Without a body of tasting notes, treat a Dehong cake as you would any unknown young sheng: small amount, short steeps, and judge the bitterness and sweetness for yourself.

Buy it for curiosity and value, and ask the seller for the county and the year. If a wrapper leans on bold claims about the region, weigh them lightly.
history: Little is documented about Dehong pu-erh as a historic tea. Chinese consumer guides now list it among known pu-erh areas, with a reported garden area of 345,000 mu, while tea writing in English treats it as a sparse area north of Lincang.
